description: Make matching team headshots in one shared light, crop and backdrop, each from a teammate's own photo. AI portraits for About and team pages.
h1: AI Team Headshots That Match, from Founder to New Hire
lead: A team page stitched together from selfies and cropped wedding shots makes a business look small, and getting everyone into one studio is a scheduling nightmare. Give each person a matching headshot made from their own approved photo.
intro: The example shows a smiling team member in a black blazer, framed from the chest up in a bright office with a plant and soft daylight behind her.

Small shops often have a Team or About page with photos taken years apart in different rooms. Matching headshots make that page look tidy and help customers put a face to the people who pack their orders and answer their emails. The Team Headshots template works best when each person uploads a recent photo and you use one setting description for everyone.
tip: Ask each person for a front-facing photo in daylight with nothing covering their face, and paste the same setting description for every headshot.

maker.upload_title: Drop a photo of the person here

faq.a: Use a recent photo of that person’s face and shoulders with even light and no hat, sunglasses or hand covering the face. Ask for consent for the specific business pages where the portrait will appear.

faq.q: How can a team page feel consistent?
faq.a: Reuse the same backdrop, crop, light direction and outfit description while letting each person keep their own portrait. A shared brief creates consistency without flattening different faces into one identity.

faq.q: Can I add names in the headshot?
faq.a: Add names and job titles as editable text beside each image on your page. Keep the portrait free of baked-in labels so you can correct a role or update a team member later.

faq.q: Can each person upload a different style of photo?
faq.a: They can, but give the team one brief: plain background, similar framing and even light. Review each image for consistent shoulders and headroom before placing the set on the public page.

faq.q: What if I need a headshot of a specific person exactly?
faq.a: The output follows the uploaded person’s visible features, but it is not an official identity document. Upload the clearest front-facing photo, ask the person to review it, and publish only with their approval.

faq.q: How much do team headshots cost?
faq.a: Each portrait costs 24 credits, so the total scales with the number of teammates. The current cost is shown before creation; make one test portrait first if you need to confirm the shared brief. Keep the approval record with the final file and page copy.

faq.q: How do I publish team portraits safely?
faq.a: Ask each person to approve the portrait and the page where it will appear. Keep the source and consent record with your team files, publish names and roles as editable text, and remove a portrait when its owner asks.

faq.q: What details belong beside each portrait?
faq.a: Use the person’s approved name, role, pronouns and a useful contact or bio sentence beside the image. Keep claims current and avoid baking a title or label into the pixels so updates stay easy. Check spelling, pronouns, role and contact destination with the person before publishing, and keep the portrait paired with the text record that can be updated later.

faq.q: Do I need permission from each teammate?
faq.a: Yes. Use a photo the person has approved for this business use, show them the finished portrait and publish only with their consent; remove a portrait if its owner asks.

faq.q: Can I use the headshots beyond the About page?
faq.a: Yes. Downloaded portraits carry no watermark and can be used on LinkedIn, pitch decks, speaker bios and other business materials, with each person's approval kept on file.

visual.overview: A matching team set helps customers recognize the people behind a small shop across its About page, support replies and founder profiles. Ask each teammate for a recent, approved photo, then reuse one brief for the crop, light, backdrop and clothing level. Keep facial features, hair and skin tone faithful to the supplied person; the generated portrait is a presentation aid, not an employee record. Let every person review their own result before it goes public, and add names, roles, pronouns and contact context as editable page text. Keep a private approval trail with the source and final portrait so a role change or removal request can be handled quickly. Review the grid at the size visitors will actually see.

steps.prompt: Use the uploaded photo as an identity reference. Retain the person’s facial features, hair, and skin tone while creating a square team headshot against a soft light-gray background, with head and shoulders in frame. Use a black blazer, white top, natural skin texture, and even daylight; no props, text, or logos. Keep the expression relaxed and the crop consistent with the rest of the team. End on a clean portrait that the person can approve before publication. Leave enough headroom for a profile card and avoid adding names or job titles inside the image. Keep the background quiet enough for readable surrounding text.

picker.title: Choose a team portrait setting
picker.lead: Pick a studio or workplace setting that keeps every face clear. Reuse a consistent crop and light direction so different source photos read as one team while each person remains recognizable. Keep each person’s approved portrait paired with their current role and contact context. A calm background leaves space for a short bio beside the image.
